title: Who Owns This Risk?
blurb: Three lines of defence, plus the body that carries ultimate accountability. Sort each activity onto its owner.
source: IIA Three Lines Model (2020) · ISO/IEC 42001:2023 §5 (leadership) · NIST AI RMF 1.0 GOVERN 2
hint: Drag each activity onto the line that should perform it. The test is independence: who can mark their own homework, and who cannot.
note: The lines are about independence, not seniority or headcount. A second-line function that reports to the team it oversees is a first-line function wearing a different badge.

zones.name: First line
zones.def: Owns and manages the risk day to day: the teams that build, deploy and operate the system.

zones.name: Second line
zones.def: Sets policy, advises, challenges and monitors — risk, compliance, legal, an AI governance function. Independent of delivery, not of management.

zones.name: Third line
zones.def: Internal audit. Independent assurance to the board on whether the first two lines actually work.

zones.name: Board / accountable executive
zones.def: Sets appetite, holds ultimate accountability, and is the only body that can accept risk beyond delegated limits.

items.label: The engineering team runs the fairness evaluation suite before promoting a model to production.
items.why: Executing controls inside the delivery process is first-line work. Doing it well does not make it assurance, because the team is assessing its own output.

items.label: The product owner records a new risk in the register and proposes a treatment.
items.why: Risk identification and day-to-day management sit with the people closest to the activity. The register is theirs to populate, not the risk function's.

items.label: The operations team monitors production drift dashboards and raises an incident when thresholds are breached.
items.why: Operating a control, including a detective one, is first-line. Second line asks whether the threshold is right; first line acts when it trips.

items.label: The data science team documents model limitations and intended use in the model card.
items.why: Producing the documentation is a build activity. Reviewing whether it meets policy is a different line's job.

items.label: The AI governance function writes the policy defining which use cases require an impact assessment.
items.why: Setting the framework and standards the first line must work within is the defining second-line activity.

items.label: Compliance reviews a completed impact assessment and challenges the team's residual risk rating.
items.why: Independent challenge of first-line judgement is second line. It is advisory and monitoring, and it is not assurance to the board.

items.label: Legal advises that a proposed deployment falls within an Annex III area and therefore attracts high-risk obligations.
items.why: Specialist advice that constrains what the first line may do is second-line. The decision to proceed remains the first line's, within policy.

items.label: The risk function maintains the enterprise register and reports aggregate AI risk exposure to the executive.
items.why: Aggregation, oversight and reporting across the first line is second-line monitoring. It relies on first-line data, which is precisely why third line exists.

items.label: Internal audit examines whether the model approval process was followed for every release in the last year.
items.why: Testing whether the controls operated as designed, after the fact and independently, is internal audit's remit.

items.label: An independent review reports to the audit committee that the second line's challenge process is not evidenced.
items.why: Third line audits the second line as well as the first, and reports to the board rather than to management — that reporting line is what makes it independent.

items.label: Assurance work is planned on a risk-based cycle and its scope is agreed with the audit committee, not with the teams being audited.
items.why: Scope set outside management is the structural feature that separates audit from a second-line review.

items.label: A review concludes that a control is documented but has never actually been performed, and reports it upward.
items.why: Finding the gap between documented and operating effectiveness is the value audit adds. Neither of the first two lines is positioned to report it against itself.

items.label: Risk appetite for automated decision-making is set and published.
items.why: Appetite is a board-level statement of how much risk the organisation will take. Everything below is calibration against it.

items.label: A residual risk exceeding the delegated limit is escalated and formally accepted at the top of the organisation.
items.why: Only the body holding the authority may accept beyond delegated limits. Acceptance elsewhere is not acceptance; it is an unrecorded exposure.

items.label: An accountable executive is named for the AI management system, with the authority and resources to make it work.
items.why: Management-system standards require named leadership accountability. A governance function with no executive owner has responsibility without authority.

items.label: The decision is taken to withdraw a deployed system after assurance reports that its risk cannot be brought within appetite.
items.why: Withdrawal against commercial interest is a decision only the accountable level can take, which is why the escalation route has to exist before it is needed.
